posts.quote: EVERY KID ON THE BLOCK KNEW THE SAME JUMP ROPE RHYMES, AND NOBODY EVER WROTE ONE DOWN.
posts.caption: Two girls turned the rope, one jumped, and the rest of the block stood in line chanting before anybody explained the rules. The rhymes had been handed down from older kids who got them from older kids before that. Nobody could tell you who made them up, and nobody ever wrote one down. Some of them made no sense at all, and you knew every word anyway. The rope slapped the sidewalk in perfect time and you counted until somebody tripped. Then the next kid stepped in, and the rhyme started over from the top.
posts.first: We had one that went on for nearly a full minute and ended with how many babies you'd have. I can still do the whole thing without a single stumble. Funny what the mind holds on to for sixty years.

posts.quote: THE KITCHEN CALENDAR CAME FREE FROM THE BANK, AND IT RAN THE WHOLE FAMILY'S LIFE IN PENCIL.
posts.caption: It hung on the kitchen wall next to the telephone, right where everybody walked past it all day. The bank gave it away every December, and Mom treated it like a ledger. Dentist appointments, birthdays, who had the car on Thursday, all of it in her small pencil handwriting. A pencil dangled from a string so nobody had an excuse. If it wasn't on the calendar, it wasn't happening. And if it was on the calendar, you could count on Mom having already circled it twice.
posts.first: Our calendar had a picture of a covered bridge on it every single year, and I don't think the bank ever changed it. Mom wrote 'Dad's birthday' on the wrong day once, and nobody ever let her forget it. I'd give anything to see that pencil handwriting again.

posts.quote: DAD FELL ASLEEP IN HIS RECLINER AFTER SUPPER, AND THE WHOLE HOUSE TIPTOED AROUND HIM LIKE A SLEEPING BEAR.
posts.caption: Supper dishes were barely cleared when Dad settled into his recliner with the evening paper. Within four minutes the paper was rising and falling on his chest and the snoring had started. Every kid in the house knew the rules without being told. You walked on the sides of your feet, you turned the television down to a whisper, and you did not ask him anything. The dog knew better than all of us and stayed well out of reach. When he finally woke up, he'd say he was only resting his eyes.
posts.first: My father swore for forty years he never slept in that chair. We have a whole stack of photographs that say otherwise. I'd tiptoe around that chair again in a heartbeat.

posts.quote: What did your mother say that you swore you'd never repeat, and then heard yourself saying to your own kids?
posts.first: Mine said 'because I said so' with a straight face every time. I swore up and down I would never say it. My oldest heard it from me before she could drive, and I heard my mother's voice come right out of my mouth.

posts.character: Lost school subjects (the old school desk)
posts.quote: THE DESK HAD AN INKWELL HOLE, SOMEBODY'S INITIALS, AND A PIECE OF GUM FROM BEFORE YOU WERE BORN.
posts.caption: Every desk in the room came bolted to a cast iron frame, and nobody could remember a time it hadn't been there. The wooden top was worn smooth in the middle from a hundred years of elbows. There was a little round hole in the corner where an inkwell used to sit. Somebody had carved a heart, somebody else had carved a name, and the underside held a gum collection that might have been historic. You got the desk you got, and you learned to keep your pencils from rolling down the slope. The teacher checked under every one of them on the last day of school.
posts.first: The desk I got in fourth grade had a set of initials carved on it that matched my uncle's. I asked him about it years later and he just grinned and changed the subject. Some secrets stayed in the classroom.

posts.quote: THE SCHOOL BUS / NO SEAT BELTS, NO ASSIGNED SEATS, AND THE BACK ROW WAS FOR THE BIG KIDS
posts.caption: The bus came around the corner at 7:20 sharp, and you had better already be standing at the end of the driveway. Mr. Hal had driven that route longer than anybody could remember. He knew every kid by name and every kid's mother by reputation. There were no seat belts and no assigned seats, only an understanding that the back rows belonged to the big kids. The little ones sat up front where he could keep an eye on them in that giant mirror. Nobody got off the bus without hearing a goodbye, and nobody got on without a good morning.
posts.first: Our driver had a coffee thermos bolted to the dashboard and a whistle that could stop any fight in the back. I sat in the third seat on the left for six straight years. I still look for that seat when I ride a bus.

posts.character: Values and work ethic (the hand-me-down coat)
posts.quote: THE COAT WAS MY BROTHER'S, THEN MINE, THEN MY SISTER'S, AND IT STILL HAD ANOTHER WINTER IN IT.
posts.caption: The coat showed up at the end of every October in the same cardboard box. Plaid wool, brass buttons, and sleeves that had been turned up and let down so many times they had permanent creases. Mom knelt in the front hall and rolled the cuffs until your hands came out. It was too big this year and it would be too small by spring, and nobody ever said a word about it. Somebody's name was written in the collar in laundry marker, and then somebody else's under it. It kept three kids warm through three winters, and it still looked pretty good.
posts.first: My coat had my older brother's name in the collar, and my cousin's name under his. I was so proud when I finally had it to myself, and then I outgrew it that spring. Mom folded it and put it in the box for the next kid down the line.

posts.quote: THE ROCKING HORSE WAS WORN SMOOTH ON THE EARS, AND EVERY KID IN THE FAMILY HAD RIDDEN IT TO THE END OF THE WORLD.
posts.caption: It stood in the corner of the sitting room, and nobody could say who had bought it or when. The paint on the mane had worn away where small hands held on. The ears were rubbed smooth from a generation of kids steering with them. You climbed on, grabbed hold, and rocked until the floor creaked and the whole house knew you were off on an adventure. Some days it was a cavalry charge and some days it was a stagecoach. And when you finally got too big for it, your little cousin was already waiting for a turn.
posts.first: That horse went through six kids in our family before it came to me. My mother still has it in her attic, one ear a little chewed, the tail held on with a knot. I stood in front of it a while last year before I could bring myself to leave.

posts.quote: What was the one chore you hated as a kid that you'd happily do again just to be back in that house?
posts.first: I hated carrying in the firewood every evening, and I would carry it a hundred times over to feel that warm kitchen again. Dad would be at the table with the paper and Mom would be at the stove. Funny what you miss.

posts.quote: GRANDMA'S PURSE HAD A HANKIE, A PEPPERMINT, A SAFETY PIN, AND AN ANSWER FOR EVERYTHING.
posts.caption: Grandma's purse was black, square, and heavy enough to be classified as a weapon. When you were scraped, there was a hankie in there that she moistened and used on your knee. If you were restless in church, a peppermint appeared and the sermon went by. Torn hem, popped button, runny nose, a safety pin handled the first two and the hankie covered the third. She would snap that clasp shut like she had just won a case. And you would still wonder where she kept it all.
posts.first: I once saw my grandmother pull a screwdriver out of that purse to fix a loose hinge in the church hall. She handed it back to the man, snapped the clasp shut, and never said a word. I think she kept the whole world in there.
